questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Expected false alarms above a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a detection threshold controls the false alarm rate
questions.stem: North arrow note 18 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why a threshold placed far from the mean of a noisy surface produces far fewer false alarms.

answer.exemplar: A noisy measured surface is treated as a random variable with a mean and a standard deviation, and a threshold is placed a number of standard deviations above the mean. If the noise is Gaussian, the fraction of readings above a threshold k standard deviations away is the tail integral, approximately the exponential factor exp of minus k squared over two. With a hundred thousand candidate readings, a threshold three standard deviations out admits only about eleven false alarms, while a threshold two standard deviations out admits more than two thousand. Choosing the threshold therefore trades missed real features against a rapidly growing false alarm count, and the exponential tail explains why the choice is so consequential.

questions.explanation: The number of readings beyond a threshold set k standard deviations out falls as the exponential of minus k squared over two, so raising the threshold cuts false alarms dramatically. A linear tail estimate would miss this steep dependence.
questions.hint: The Gaussian tail falls exponentially in k squared.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Band gap behind an emission wavelength
questions.learningObjective: Explain how photon energy follows from a plotted wavelength
questions.stem: Compass note 27 asks the cartographer to explain in writing how the energy of a photon follows from the wavelength recorded on the chart.

answer.exemplar: A photon carries energy E = h f, where f is the frequency of the light. Since the frequency of light is the speed of light divided by the wavelength, the energy can be written as the Planck constant times the speed of light divided by the wavelength, which gives the useful rule of thumb that the energy in electron volts is 1240 divided by the wavelength in nanometres. The relation is therefore an inverse one: a short wavelength such as deep blue near 450 nm means a photon of about 2.8 eV, while a long wavelength such as 1200 nm in the infrared means about 1.0 eV. Every colour on a chart can thus be read as an energy scale.

questions.explanation: Photon energy is the Planck constant times the frequency, and frequency is the speed of light over the wavelength, so energy falls as wavelength grows. The rule of thumb of 1240 eV nm converts any plotted wavelength to energy.
questions.hint: Energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Heat capacity of an ideal gas in terms of mode count
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an ideal gas heat capacity follows the mode count
questions.stem: Legend footnote 6 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why the heat capacity of an ideal gas is set by the number of active modes rather than by the amount of gas alone.

answer.exemplar: In the classical picture each quadratic term in the energy of a molecule holds on average one half of kT, so a molecule with f independent quadratic modes has an internal energy of f kT over two. The constant volume heat capacity is the derivative of that energy with respect to temperature, which for one mole is f R over two, and for n moles it is n f R over two. A monatomic gas has three translational modes and gives (3/2)R, while a diatomic gas adds two rotational modes and gives (5/2)R if the vibrational mode stays frozen out. The mode count therefore fixes the heat capacity, and the amount of gas only multiplies it.

questions.explanation: Equipartition gives half of kT per active quadratic mode, so the constant volume heat capacity is n f R over two. The mode count fixes the value for a mole, and the number of moles only multiplies it.
questions.hint: Count modes, then multiply by moles.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Combining two independent random uncertainties
questions.learningObjective: Explain why independent errors combine in quadrature
questions.stem: Triangulation note 22 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why independent errors are combined in quadrature rather than added.

answer.exemplar: Each independent measurement carries a random error whose sign is as likely to be positive as negative, so the errors do not accumulate in one direction. When several such independent errors enter the same result, the cross products between different errors average to zero over many repetitions, and the variance of the sum is therefore the sum of the individual variances. The standard deviation of the combined result is the square root of the sum of the individual standard deviations squared. Adding the errors linearly instead would assume that they always point the same way and would badly overstate the uncertainty, which matters greatly when a contour is interpolated between spot heights.

questions.explanation: Independent errors have random signs, so their cross products cancel on averaging and the variances add. Taking the root of the summed squares is the correct combination, and a linear sum overstates the uncertainty.
questions.hint: Variances add, so take the root of the sum.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Efficiency of a solar cell
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the efficiency of a cell is measured
questions.stem: North line note 17 asks the cartographer to explain in writing how the efficiency of a photovoltaic cell is measured and why the fill factor appears.

answer.exemplar: The efficiency of a cell is the electrical power it delivers divided by the solar power falling on it, so the incident power must be measured over the same area as the cell and with the same spectrum. The delivered power is taken from the current-voltage curve at the working point rather than at its maximum, and the fill factor is the ratio of that operating power to the product of the open circuit voltage and the short circuit current. Because the curve is rounded rather than rectangular, the fill factor is below one, typically around 0.75 to 0.85 for a good silicon cell. The remaining losses are absorbed in the reflection from the surface, in the recombination of carriers and in the resistance of the contacts.

questions.explanation: Efficiency compares the operating power from the current-voltage curve with the solar power on the cell, and the fill factor accounts for how far the curve falls short of its rectangular ideal. Reflection and recombination reduce the result further.
questions.hint: Output from the curve over incident power.

questions.stem: Spot height note 23 asks the cartographer to explain in writing how the uncertainty of a position derived from several independent observations should be quoted.

answer.exemplar: Each observation of a position carries an independent random uncertainty, and because the errors have random signs the cross terms between different observations average to zero. The variance of the combined position is therefore the sum of the individual variances, and the combined standard uncertainty is the square root of that sum. This is why the quoted uncertainty of a triangulated point is smaller than the uncertainty of any single observation but never smaller than the smallest one, and it is why an averaged map detail carries a reliability that a single fix does not. questions.hint: Add variances, then take the root.

questions.topic: Efficiency of a solar cell
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the efficiency of a cell falls as the panel warms
questions.stem: Graticule bubble note 7 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why the efficiency of a cell falls as the temperature of the panel rises.

answer.exemplar: The open circuit voltage of a cell falls with temperature, and since the current at the working point changes far less, the delivered power and the efficiency both drop. Two effects set this. The reverse saturation current of the junction grows exponentially with temperature, roughly doubling for every ten kelvin rise, which drains current from the device. At the same time the voltage needed to overcome the built in barrier falls by a fixed amount per kelvin, so the maximum available voltage shrinks. A cell rated at about half a percent per kelvin therefore loses several percent of its efficiency between the cool morning and the warm afternoon, which is why panels are rated at standard test conditions.

questions.explanation: The reverse saturation current grows rapidly with temperature while the open circuit voltage falls, so the delivered power and the efficiency both drop as the panel warms. The current effect is exponential, so a modest warming costs real output.
questions.hint: The voltage falls and the dark current grows.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Response time of a smoothing filter
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a smoothing filter does to fine detail
questions.stem: Projection bubble note 16 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why a smoothing filter reduces the high frequency detail on a contour and what sets the amount of smoothing.

answer.exemplar: A smoothing filter replaces each sample with a weighted average of its neighbours, which spreads a sharp change over several samples. The high frequency content of a rugged surface is precisely the part that changes quickly from one sample to the next, so averaging attenuates it most strongly while leaving the broad shape of the terrain intact. In a simple electrical implementation the average is produced by a resistor and capacitor pair, and the amount of smoothing is set by the time constant of that pair, with a longer time constant giving a longer memory and heavier smoothing. Choosing the time constant is therefore a trade between suppressing noise, which keeps the contour readable, and preserving genuine sharp features such as a narrow ridge.

questions.explanation: Averaging neighbouring samples attenuates the fastest changes most, so rugged detail is flattened while the broad shape survives. The amount of smoothing is set by the memory or time constant of the filter.
questions.hint: Fast changes are averaged away first.

questions.topic: Attenuation of light along a fibre
questions.learningObjective: Explain how light is attenuated along a fibre
questions.stem: Projection margin note 13 asks the cartographer to explain in writing how light loses power along an optical fibre and why the loss is stated in decibels.

answer.exemplar: As light travels along a fibre it is scattered out of the core by microscopic imperfections, and it is also absorbed where the material has impurities. Both processes remove power from the guided beam, and the loss per unit length is called the attenuation. Because the light is a wave, engineers quote this loss on a logarithmic scale, in decibels per kilometre, so that a long route made of many identical fibre sections can be added up in simple arithmetic and compared directly with the power budget of the transmitter. A loss of 3 dB corresponds to the power being halved over that length, and a route of 20 km at 0.25 dB per kilometre attenuates by 5 dB in total, halving the power five times over.

questions.explanation: Scattering and absorption remove power from the guided beam, and the logarithmic decibel scale lets losses along a long route be added directly. A loss of 3 dB halves the power over that length.
questions.hint: Decibels add over the length of the route.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: The spread relation for diffusion
questions.learningObjective: Explain the square root growth of a diffusive spread
questions.stem: Projection note 21 asks the cartographer to explain in writing why the spread of a diffusing tracer grows with the square root of time rather than with time itself.

answer.exemplar: A tracer that diffuses performs many independent random steps, each of length l, and in a time t it makes a number of steps N that is proportional to t. The mean square displacement is N times l squared, because the cross terms between different steps cancel on averaging, and the constant of proportionality is the diffusion constant. The rms spread is the square root of that mean square displacement, so it grows as the square root of t. The physical picture is that adding more steps does not add to the distance travelled, since the steps point in random directions, and the spread of a random walk is governed by the square root of the number of steps.

questions.explanation: Random steps make the mean square displacement proportional to the number of steps, which grows linearly with time, so the rms spread grows as the square root of time. Steps do not add because their directions are random.
questions.hint: Steps add in quadrature, not in a straight line.

options.misconception: drops the fill factor from the power calculation

options.text: The output is 3.00 W and the efficiency is 15.0 percent.
options.misconception: uses the open circuit voltage times the current without the fill factor

options.text: The output is 2.25 W and the efficiency is 11.25 percent.

questions.explanation: The operating power is the voltage times the current times the fill factor, that is 2.25 W, and the incident power is 1000 times 0.020, that is 20 W, so the efficiency is 11.25 percent. Leaving out the fill factor overstates the result.
questions.hint: Multiply voltage, current and fill factor.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Band gap behind an emission wavelength
questions.learningObjective: State how a plotted wavelength sets the photon energy
questions.stem: Sheet spectrum note 12 asks which statement correctly links a plotted wavelength to the energy of the photons behind it.

options.text: The energy is proportional to the wavelength, so a longer plotted line carries more energy per photon.
options.misconception: makes the energy grow with the wavelength

options.text: The energy is proportional to the square of the wavelength, since the energy scales with the wave amplitude.
options.misconception: invokes a square law that does not describe photons

options.text: The energy is inversely proportional to the wavelength, with the constant of proportionality 1240 eV nm.
The energy is the inverse of the frequency, since a faster wave carries less energy per photon.
options.misconception: inverts the relation between frequency and photon energy

questions.explanation: Photon energy is the Planck constant times the frequency, and frequency is the speed of light over the wavelength, so the energy falls as the wavelength grows, with the constant 1240 eV nm. Making the energy grow with wavelength reverses the relation.
questions.hint: Longer waves, lower energy.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Attenuation of light along a fibre
questions.learningObjective: Derive a per-kilometre loss from an end to end power measurement
questions.stem: Route note 19 gives the measured power at the far end of a 40 km fibre route as 0.02 mW when 1.00 mW is launched, and asks for the loss per kilometre.

options.text: The total loss is 50 dB, which is 1.25 dB per kilometre over the 40 km route.
options.misconception: reads the power ratio of fifty as a decibel value

options.text: The total loss is 16.99 dB, which is 0.42 dB over the whole 40 km route.
options.misconception: reports the total loss but forgets to divide by the route length

options.text: The total loss is 1.70 dB, which is 0.0425 dB per kilometre over the 40 km route.
options.misconception: misses the factor of ten in the decibel conversion

options.text: The total loss is 16.99 dB, which is 0.425 dB per kilometre over the 40 km route.

questions.explanation: The total loss is ten times the logarithm of the power ratio, that is 16.99 dB, and over 40 km that is 0.425 dB per kilometre. Reading the ratio of fifty as a decibel value would give a very different answer.
questions.hint: Decibels total, then divide by the distance.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Combining two independent random uncertainties
questions.learningObjective: Combine four independent closure errors into one uncertainty
questions.stem: Datum note 4 lists four independent errors of 8 m, 15 m, 20 m and 11 m and asks for the combined standard uncertainty of the adjusted station.
questions.explanation: The variances add, so the combined uncertainty is the square root of 810, which is 28.46 m. Adding the four errors directly would give 54 m, a much more pessimistic figure.
questions.hint: Root of the sum of the four squares.
